questions.stem: An older adult takes ibuprofen daily for osteoarthritis and low-dose aspirin for secondary cardiovascular prevention. Which new finding requires the most urgent follow-up?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"New epigastric burning after meals today with no change in stool color and no dizziness when the client stands.","B":"A black, tarry stool accompanied by new lightheadedness and a measurable drop in blood pressure when standing now.","C":"Several small forearm bruises after minor bumps without gum bleeding, hematuria, or a change in the client's energy level.","D":"Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day with stable weight, clear lung sounds, and unchanged exercise tolerance."}}
questions.rationale: NSAIDs can cause serious gastrointestinal bleeding at any time, and older adults are at greater risk. Black, tarry stool plus orthostatic lightheadedness is concerning for clinically significant gastrointestinal blood loss and requires prompt evaluation. Concomitant ibuprofen also warrants review in a client using aspirin for cardiovascular protection.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Ibuprofen Tablets (updated Jan. 5, 2026) + FDA Ibuprofen/Aspirin Safety Information
questions.source_detail: DailyMed boxed warning: serious GI bleeding can occur without warning and elderly patients are at greater risk. FDA also advises review of timing/combined use of ibuprofen and aspirin.

questions.stem: A client with a 6-week cough, night sweats, weight loss, and an upper-lobe cavitary lesion is admitted to a semiprivate room. Pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the client in a private positive-pressure room and have staff wear surgical masks while diagnostic testing is pending.","B":"Keep the client in the semiprivate room, apply droplet precautions, and move the roommate later if sputum testing confirms tuberculosis.","C":"Apply source control to the client, move the client to an airborne infection isolation room, and use a fit-tested respirator for care.","D":"Place the client on contact precautions in a private room and use gown and gloves until three sputum specimens have been collected."}}
questions.rationale: Suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis requires Airborne Precautions. CDC guidance calls for source control, placement in an airborne infection isolation room when available, and respiratory protection for healthcare personnel. Confirmation by sputum testing is not required before initiating these precautions.
questions.source_name: CDC — Tuberculosis Infection Control / Transmission-Based Precautions
questions.source_detail: CDC: prompt detection of presumed TB, Airborne Precautions, AIIR placement, and respiratory protective equipment such as a fit-tested N95.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client has laboratory-confirmed seasonal influenza and is coughing frequently. Which infection-control plan is appropriate during routine care?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use Standard plus Droplet Precautions, including a mask for healthcare personnel during close care and source control for transport.","B":"Use Standard plus Airborne Precautions with an N95 respirator for all routine care until every respiratory symptom has resolved.","C":"Use Standard plus Contact Precautions with gown and gloves for all room entry because influenza spreads mainly through surfaces.","D":"Use Standard Precautions alone once antiviral therapy begins because treatment promptly removes the need for transmission-based precautions."}}
questions.rationale: CDC guidance for seasonal influenza in healthcare settings requires Standard Precautions plus Droplet Precautions for suspected or confirmed influenza. Airborne infection isolation is not routinely required for ordinary influenza care, although respiratory protection may be indicated for aerosol-generating procedures under facility guidance.
questions.source_name: CDC — Influenza Infection Control in Health Care Facilities (May 8, 2026)
questions.source_detail: Current CDC influenza guidance continues Standard plus Droplet Precautions for suspected or confirmed seasonal influenza.

questions.stem: An inpatient in an acute-care hospital is known to be colonized with MRSA and is on Contact Precautions. Which PPE approach is most appropriate for routine bedside care?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wear a surgical mask and eye protection for every room entry, adding gloves when contact with body fluids is anticipated.","B":"Wear an N95 respirator for bedside care and add a gown when the client has respiratory symptoms or an uncovered wound.","C":"Wear gloves for routine care and add a gown when direct client contact is expected, but not for contact with equipment or surfaces.","D":"Wear gown and gloves for care involving contact with the client or nearby environment, then remove them before leaving the room."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends Contact Precautions for acute-care inpatients colonized or infected with MRSA. Contact Precautions include gown and gloves for interactions that may involve contact with the patient or the patient's environment, followed by appropriate doffing and hand hygiene.
questions.source_name: CDC — Preventing MRSA in Healthcare Facilities
questions.source_detail: CDC acute-care guidance: patients colonized or infected with MRSA should be managed with Contact Precautions; gown and gloves are used for relevant patient/environment contact.

questions.stem: A nurse removes gloves after providing perineal care. The nurse's hands are not visibly soiled, and another patient requires a blood-pressure check next. What should the nurse do?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Proceed directly to the next patient because intact gloves prevented meaningful contamination of the nurse's hands during the previous care.","B":"Perform hand hygiene immediately after glove removal, using an alcohol-based hand rub unless another indication requires soap and water.","C":"Wash with soap and water for every glove removal because alcohol-based hand rub is not recommended after contact with body fluids.","D":"Delay hand hygiene until after the blood-pressure check because hand hygiene is primarily required before aseptic or invasive procedures."}}
questions.rationale: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. CDC recommends hand hygiene immediately after glove removal and after contact with blood or body fluids. When hands are not visibly soiled, alcohol-based hand rub is preferred in most routine clinical situations unless a specific indication calls for soap and water.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
questions.source_detail: CDC indications include immediately after glove removal, after body-fluid contact, after patient contact, and before patient contact; ABHS is preferred in most routine care when hands are not visibly soiled.
